In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ratio adjusted estimator has the same bias as the design-based estimator but a variance which is smaller by an amount that increases with the reliability of the auxiliary variable estimate.
the ratio adjusted estimator can be recommended for small areas with a high degree of confidence.

the ratio adjusted estimator can be recommended for small area estimation when the population of the area of interest is less than about one-third of the total population of the large area, and when the ratio is estimated from a sample that is large relative to the population of the small area.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the ratio adjusted estimator has lower mean squared error for small areas than the design-based estimator, provided that the ratio adjustment is based on a large area with a population size at least 10 times the size of the small area and the ratio of the small area to the large area is at least 0.1.

the efficiency of design based estimators for small area estimation can be improved by using a large area auxiliary variable total as a ratio adjustment, provided that there is a high correlation between the auxiliary variable totals for small and large area.
, for a given level of accuracy, the ratio adjustment reduces the sample size by about 50% for small areas and by about 30% for large areas.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the bias of the ratio estimator is negligible and its variance is smaller than the variance of the unadjusted estimator, provided that the ratio is not too far from unity.
the ratio adjustment can be a good alternative for small area estimation when the auxiliary variable is not highly correlated with the attribute of interest.
, for large area surveys, the ratio adjusted estimator may not be efficient.
